# Why We Plot {background-color="#007155"}

## Four Datasets, One Set of Statistics {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
anscombe_long <- anscombe |>
  pivot_longer(everything(),
               names_to = c(".value", "set"),
               names_pattern = "(.)(.)") |>
  mutate(set = paste("Dataset", set))

anscombe_long |>
  group_by(set) |>
  summarize(
    mean_x = mean(x), mean_y = mean(y),
    sd_x = sd(x), sd_y = sd(y),
    correlation = cor(x, y)
  ) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(v) round(v, 2))) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

- This is **Anscombe's quartet** (1973), built into R as `anscombe`
- Same means, same standard deviations, same correlation. Are these the same data?

## Not Even Close {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(anscombe_long, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "#007155") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "gray40",
              formula = y ~ x) +
  facet_wrap(~ set)
```

- One linear trend, one curve, one outlier dragging the line, and one single point doing all the work
- Summary statistics are a compression. A chart is often the fastest way to see what the compression might've overlooked.
- These four charts came from a few lines of `ggplot2` code. By the end of tonight you'll be able to write them yourself, starting with how ggplot2 thinks about a chart.

# The Grammar of Graphics {background-color="#007155"}

## Every ggplot Has Three Parts {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="70%"}
1. **Data**: a data frame, one row per observation (this is why we `pivot_longer`)
2. **Aesthetics** `aes()`: which columns map to which visual properties, like x position, y position, color, or size
3. **Geoms**: the shapes that actually get drawn, like points, bars, lines, or boxes

Everything else (facets, scales, labels, themes) refines those three. R4DS [Ch. 9](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/layers) calls this a *layered grammar*, because you build a plot by adding layers with `+`
:::

::: {.column width="30%"}
![](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/logo.png)
:::

::::

## Tonight's Data: `midwest`, Again {.smaller}

```{r}
midwest_df <- midwest |>
  select(county, state, poptotal, popdensity, percollege,
         percbelowpoverty, inmetro)

midwest_df
```

- The same 437 Midwestern counties from Week 2, from the 2000 Census
- `<-` saves the result as a new object, `midwest_df`. Assigning prints nothing, so the second line just types the name to show it.
- Every chart tonight starts from `midwest_df`. Look for it in your Environment pane.
- `inmetro` is `1` for counties in a metro area and `0` otherwise

## Step 1: Just the Data {.smaller}

```{r}
ggplot(midwest_df)
```

- A blank canvas. ggplot knows the data, but not what to draw or where

## Step 2: Add Aesthetics {.smaller}

```{r}
base_plot <- ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percollege, y = percbelowpoverty))

base_plot
```

- Now it knows which column goes on which axis, so it draws the axes and scales. Still no data on the plot.
- A plot is an object too, so we can save it as `base_plot` and build on it

## Step 3: Add a Geom {.smaller}

```{r}
base_plot +
  geom_point()
```

- `base_plot` already holds the data and aesthetics. `+ geom_point()` adds the layer that draws one point per row.
- `base_plot` itself hasn't changed. To keep the new version, assign it: `scatter <- base_plot + geom_point()`.
- A first look: more college grads, somewhat less poverty, but lots of scatter

## Mapping a Third Variable to Color {.smaller}

```{r}
ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percollege, y = percbelowpoverty, color = state)) +
  geom_point()
```

- Anything inside `aes()` is **mapped** to a column, and ggplot builds the legend for you
- Five colors is about the limit before a chart gets hard to read

## Mapping vs. Setting {.smaller}

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: "80%"
ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percollege, y = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = inmetro))

ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percollege, y = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue")
```

- **Left, mapped**: inside `aes()`, color comes from a column, with a legend
- **Right, set**: outside `aes()`, one fixed color and no legend
- `inmetro` is stored as a number, so ggplot gives it a 0-to-1 color gradient even though it's only ever 0 or 1
- Rule of thumb: inside `aes()` if it depends on the data

## Layers Can Stack {.smaller}

```{r}
ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percollege, y = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x)
```

- Each `+ geom_*()` adds a layer on top of the last
- `alpha` makes points semi-transparent, so overlapping points show up darker
- `geom_smooth(method = "lm")` adds a linear trend with a confidence band (`se = FALSE` hides it)

## Global vs. Local Aesthetics {.smaller}

```{r}
ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percollege, y = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = state), alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, color = "black")
```

- Aesthetics in `ggplot()` apply to every layer
- Aesthetics in a single geom apply only to that layer
- Here, color by state for the points, but one overall trend line. Move `color = state` up into `ggplot()` and you'd get five lines instead.

## Facets: Small Multiples {.smaller}

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percollege, y = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ state)
```

- `facet_wrap()` makes one panel per value of a variable, all on the same scales
- Often easier to read than five colors crammed into one panel

## Labels Make It Readable {.smaller}

```{r}
ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percollege, y = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "#007155") +
  labs(
    title = "More college grads, less poverty",
    subtitle = "Midwestern counties, 2000 Census",
    x = "Adults with a college degree (%)",
    y = "Population below poverty line (%)",
    caption = "Source: ggplot2::midwest"
  )
```

- Column names like `percbelowpoverty` are fine for you. They are not fine for anyone else.
- A title that states the finding does more work than one that restates the axes

## The Template {.smaller}

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(data = <DATA>, aes(<MAPPINGS>)) +
  <GEOM_FUNCTION>() +
  <MORE LAYERS, FACETS, LABELS>
```

- Almost every chart this semester, maps included, fits this shape
- R4DS [Ch. 9](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/layers) has the full list of geoms, and the [ggplot2 cheat sheet](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/html/data-visualization.html) is worth keeping open

# Exploratory Data Analysis {background-color="#007155"}

## What Is EDA? {.smaller}

> "Far better an approximate answer to the right question, which is often vague, than an exact answer to the wrong question, which can always be made precise."
>
> — John Tukey

- **Exploratory data analysis** is a loop, not a formal procedure:
  1. Ask a question about your data
  2. Answer it with a chart, a transformation, or a summary
  3. Use what you learned to ask a better question
- Most of these charts are for *you*. They don't need titles or polish.

## Asking Good Questions {.smaller}

- As Wickham says in Ch. 10, "EDA is fundamentally a creative process. And like most creative processes, the key to asking quality questions is to generate a large quantity of questions."
- R4DS [Ch. 10](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/EDA.html) frames it around two kinds of questions: how does a variable **vary**, and how do variables **covary**?

# Variation: One Variable at a Time {background-color="#007155"}

## Continuous Variables: Histograms {.smaller}

```{r}
ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2)
```

- A histogram cuts the x-axis into bins and counts the rows in each
- Most counties sit between about 7% and 18% in poverty, with a tail to the right

## Bin Width Changes the Story {.smaller}

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: "100%"
ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5)

ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10)
```

- Too narrow and it's noise. Too wide and the shape disappears.
- Try a few. There's no single right answer, and the default (30 bins) is not always the best one.

## Skewed Data: Try a Log Scale {.smaller}

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: "100%"
ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = poptotal)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30)

ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = poptotal)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma())
```

- **Left**: Cook County (Chicago, 5M people) squashes everything else into one bar
- **Right**: on a log scale, each step on the axis is ten times bigger than the last, and the distribution becomes readable
- County populations, incomes, and housing prices almost always need this

## Categorical Variables: Bar Charts {.smaller}

```{r}
ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = state)) +
  geom_bar()
```

- `geom_bar()` counts rows for you, the same thing `count(state)` did in Week 2
- If you already have the counts in a column, you can use `geom_col()` instead, with the counts as `y`

## Unusual Values {.smaller}

```{r}
high_poverty <- midwest_df |>
  filter(percbelowpoverty > 30) |>
  select(county, state, poptotal, percbelowpoverty)

high_poverty
```

- The long right tail from the histogram, pulled out with `filter()`
- Outliers aren't automatically errors. Check whether each one is real or a data problem. These are real: Menominee County, WI is almost entirely the Menominee Reservation, and Alexander and Pulaski are at Illinois's rural southern tip.
- Don't delete an unusual value just because it's unusual. If it's a real error, replace it with `NA` and say so.

# Covariation: How Variables Move Together {background-color="#007155"}

## Adding a Column We'll Reuse {.smaller}

```{r}
midwest_df <- midwest_df |>
  mutate(metro = if_else(inmetro == 1, "Metro", "Nonmetro"))

midwest_df |> count(metro)
```

- `inmetro`'s `1`s and `0`s make poor labels, so we add a readable `metro` column
- Assigning back to `midwest_df` overwrites it with the new version. Every chart from here on can use `metro` without repeating the `mutate()`.
- Overwriting an object is fine for adding a column. Be careful doing it with `filter()`, since dropped rows don't come back until you rerun the earlier code.

## Categorical + Continuous: Boxplots {.smaller}

```{r}
ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = metro, y = percollege)) +
  geom_boxplot()
```

- The box is the middle 50% of counties, the line is the median, and the dots are outliers
- Metro counties have a clearly higher share of college grads, and far more spread

## Reordering Categories {.smaller}

```{r}
ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = fct_reorder(state, percbelowpoverty, median),
                    y = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = NULL)
```

- By default ggplot puts categories in alphabetical order, which is almost never what you want
- `fct_reorder()` sorts them by the median of another variable, so the pattern reads left to right

## Two Categorical Variables {.smaller}

```{r}
metro_counts <- midwest_df |>
  count(state, metro)

ggplot(metro_counts, aes(x = state, y = metro, fill = n)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), color = "white", size = 6)
```

- `count()` the combinations first and save them as `metro_counts`, then draw a tile for each row of it
- A heat map like this is really just a colored table. For a handful of categories, a plain table from `count()` can work just as well.

## Two Continuous Variables {.smaller}

```{r}
ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = popdensity, y = percollege)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x)
```

- The scatterplot you already know, with a log x-axis for the same reason as before
- `method = "loess"` fits a curve instead of a straight line. It's flat across rural counties, climbs through the middle, and levels off in the densest ones. A straight line would miss that shape.

## Patterns Are Questions, Not Answers {.smaller}

When you spot a pattern, ask:

- Could it be coincidence?
- How strong is it, and how would you describe it in one sentence?
- What other variable might explain it? (Here, metro status is doing a lot of the work.)
- Does it hold within subgroups, like each state or metro vs. nonmetro?

EDA points you toward the story. It doesn't prove it.

**Note**: There are often many ways to accomplish the same task. Check out [this article](https://datavizcatalogue.com/blog/box-plot-variations/) about alternatives to boxplots.

## Saving a Plot {.smaller}

```{r}
#| eval: false
p <- ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percollege, y = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_point()

ggsave("poverty_college.png", p, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)
```

- Same idea as `base_plot` earlier: save the plot as an object, then hand that object to `ggsave()`
- `ggsave()` writes it to a file, sized in inches. Set the size on purpose so text doesn't come out tiny.
- Inside a Quarto document, you usually don't need this. The chart renders right into the HTML.

## Your Turn (20 min) {.smaller}

Using `midwest_df`, make each of these. Work with a neighbor.

1. A histogram of `percollege`. Try at least two bin widths and pick the one you think tells the story best.
2. A scatterplot of `percollege` (x) against `percbelowpoverty` (y), colored by metro status (if `metro` is missing, rerun the `mutate()` from earlier)
3. Boxplots of `percollege` by state, sorted by median
4. Take any one of the three and give it real labels with `labs()`, including a title that states what you see

## Your Turn: One Way to Do It {.smaller}

```{r}
#| eval: false
# 1
ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percollege)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2)

# 2
ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percollege, y = percbelowpoverty, color = metro)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5)

# 3
ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = fct_reorder(state, percollege, median),
                    y = percollege)) +
  geom_boxplot()

# 4
college_hist <- ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percollege)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2) +
  labs(title = "In most Midwestern counties, under 1 in 5 adults has a degree",
       x = "Adults with a college degree (%)", y = "Number of counties")

college_hist
```
